newsitem.title: USA: D.C. Mayor's new budget draws doubts.
newsitem.headline: D.C. Mayor's new budget draws doubts.

text.p: Washington DC Mayor Marion Barry Monday proposed a balanced budget for the nation's capital in the next fiscal year, a year earlier than required by Congress.

But the district's congressionally appointed chief financial officer said he would not endorse the $5 billion plan on the grounds it would be "poorly received" by Wall Street, which must market the city's bonds to help fund essential services.
Wall Street first wants the city to resolve problems such as a multibillion-dollar unfunded pension liability, chief financial officer Anthony Williams said in a letter accompanying the budget.
Congress, which has the constitutional power to oversee the nation's capital, has ordered the district to balance its budget by fiscal 1999.

But Washington and its five-member control board want to balance it in fiscal 1998 to impress Congress, which will begin reviewing a $3.9 billion, five-year federal relief package for the district developed by the White House.
Congress shifted much of the local power to a board of financial overseers, known locally as the financial oversight board, in 1995. The district is virtually insolvent.
Barry said he would continue to reduce the city's work force through restructuring, streamlining and by outsourcing services the city could no longer afford to offer.
He said debt restructuring was critical to balance the city's budget a year before the congressional requirement.
